title: Acoustic space variation and phylogenetic-allometric patterns in baleen whale vocalizations
content:
Abstract
Acoustic communication is a central behaviour in vertebrates. Vocalizations across species reflect adaptations to different ecological and social contexts, but are also influenced by evolutionary history and functional constraints. As an iconic soniferous taxon, baleen whales produce vocalizations exhibiting a wide variety of properties. These signalling behaviours may correlate with non-acoustic behaviours, including anti-predator defence (e.g. ‘flight’ or ‘fight’ behaviours). We compiled acoustic features from 1500 sounds from the literature for all baleen whale species. The acoustic space, considered here as the two-dimensional space of frequency vs. time occupied by a species’ vocalizations, was quantified, revealing that humpback whales consistently occupy the largest acoustic space, while balaenopterids occupy smaller acoustic areas. Comparative methods, including Phylogenetic Generalized Least Squares were applied to investigate the relationship between acoustic traits and body length while accounting for evolutionary history. Body length significantly explained the limits of frequency range, but had no explanatory power for the other traits when phylogeny was considered. Residual variation in acoustic traits appeared largely independent of phylogeny, suggesting that factors beyond body length and shared ancestry contribute to the observed behavioural, ecological, and acoustic diversity. It highlights the complex interplay between morphology, evolution, and acoustic trait variation in baleen whales.
